questions.q: What is the key difference between a write-off and an adjustment?
options: A write-off can only be used on miscellaneous receipts
An adjustment corrects a balance that is wrong; a write-off abandons collection of a balance that is correct
There is no real difference between the two
A write-off always increases the balance due
questions.explain: An adjustment fixes an incorrect number, while a write-off formally gives up on collecting a balance the company agrees is legitimate.

questions.q: What is a receipt write-off typically used for?
options: Writing off an entire year's worth of invoices at once
Reversing a receipt that bounced
Cleaning up a small leftover balance, such as a minor underpayment, at the point of applying a receipt
Creating a new customer account
questions.explain: A receipt write-off handles a small residual balance, like a minor underpayment, closing the transaction cleanly rather than leaving it open indefinitely.

questions.q: What typically precedes a transaction write-off?
options: A customer requesting a refund
A lockbox validation failure
An automatic receipt batch
Collections efforts that have run their course with no success
questions.explain: A transaction write-off usually happens after collections efforts have been exhausted and the customer is deemed unlikely to ever pay.

questions.q: What controls how large a write-off a given user can process without escalation?
options: The customer's credit limit
Approval limits assigned per user, by currency, with a minimum and maximum amount
The transaction's due date
The receipt method's creation method
questions.explain: Write-off approval limits, like adjustment approval limits, are defined per user and currency, capping what can be written off without escalation.

questions.q: What happens to an invoice's visibility in the system after it is written off?
options: It is permanently deleted from transaction history
It is converted into a miscellaneous receipt
It is automatically reopened the next period
It stays in transaction history for audit purposes, with its balance zeroed out
questions.explain: A written-off transaction remains visible in history so the loss can be traced and audited, even though its balance is zeroed out.
